item.title: Shelter Dog Had 48 Hours to Live. Strangers Changed That.
item.dc:creator: roccistucci
item.content:encoded:
A shelter dog rescue story doesn't usually start with a hamburger patty and a blow-dry. But Cholo's did. The 54-pound pit bull mix had roughly 48 hours left on the clock at Dallas Animal Services when a reporter showed up, took one look at those calm brown eyes, and decided to do something about it.

Background and Context

Dallas Animal Services was already stretched past its limits. In the same week that Cholo and Gojo arrived on the emergency placement list, the shelter had processed animals from three separate large-scale cruelty seizure cases, pushing an already strained facility well beyond its safe operating threshold. WFAA

That's not a freak event. It's a pattern.

As recently as April 2026, Dallas Animal Services reported 674 dogs in just 388 kennels, including 67 nursing puppies, marking the shelter's highest dog capacity in years. When a facility built for 388 animals is housing 674, the math turns brutal fast. Dogs that might otherwise get another week, another chance, another shot at a family, get put down instead. Not because they're dangerous. Because there's nowhere to put them. National Today

Nationally, animal shelters are now caring for 245,000 more companion animals than they were in 2022. The crisis isn't unique to Dallas, but Dallas is where Cholo and Gojo's clock was running out. And it's where a handful of ordinary people decided to stop scrolling and start acting. Humane World for Animals

The 48-Hour Countdown: A Shelter Dog Rescue Story Worth Telling

The Dallas90 emergency placement list is exactly what it sounds like: a triage document for dogs closest to the end. Cholo and Gojo, both 3-year-old pit bull mixes surrendered to DAS in early May, were on it. Gojo was scheduled for euthanasia the following morning. Cholo had two days.

Reporter Sarah Gupta and photographer Mackenzie Capp arrived at the shelter to find a line of would-be adopters and fosters stretching out the front door. They asked for Gojo first.

What they got was a silver-gray dog with hazel eyes and a tail that apparently hadn't received the memo about his situation. He trotted out, leapt into the car, and within minutes, a woman rolled down her window in the parking lot. She'd seen him on TikTok. She'd driven to the shelter specifically for him. Just like that, Gojo had a foster.

So they turned their attention to Cholo.

At 54 pounds, Cholo looked like the kind of dog a lot of people cross the street to avoid. He was calm, easygoing, and quiet in the back seat. One thing was clear within a few minutes: he needed a bath. A stop at White Rock Pet Grooming followed, where staff pitched in and gave him the full treatment. Cholo stood through it without complaint. He didn't bark at the dryer. He didn't flinch. He just let it happen, like a dog who'd been waiting a long time for someone to be kind to him.

His next stop was Dairy-Ette, where an employee brought out a hamburger patty just for him, snapped a photo, and offered the reporter a drink. That moment right there, a stranger feeding a condemned dog a burger because it seemed like the right thing to do, captures something the national debate about animal shelters almost always misses.

It's not policy that saves these dogs. It's people.

Dallas Animal Services Overcrowding: The Crisis Behind the Story

Victoria Chittam Bennett, assistant director of Dallas Animal Services, put it plainly: "Our shelter is beyond the population level that allows us to operate most effectively. Our staff and volunteers continue to provide compassionate care to every animal who comes through our doors, but we cannot do this alone." WFAA

That last sentence is the one that matters. They cannot do this alone.

Operation Kindness, which is led by a former DAS director, transferred 97 animals out of Dallas Animal Services in just one month, and 852 over the prior 12 months, making it DAS's leading transfer partner. Even with that kind of support, the shelter's population keeps climbing. Operation Kindness

As of late March 2024, DAS had 61 dogs on "Code Red," the designation for animals most urgently facing euthanasia due to in-shelter behavior, medical conditions, or simply a lack of space. That number reflects normal operating conditions. When cruelty seizure cases hit in clusters, the way they did the week Cholo and Gojo arrived, the backlog compounds fast. The Dallas Express

The hard truth is this: municipal shelters operate on government budgets, government timelines, and government headcounts. When the intake spikes, the options narrow. Euthanasia isn't cruelty. It's arithmetic. The only way to change the arithmetic is to get more dogs out the door faster, and that requires community engagement at a scale most city agencies can't manufacture on their own.

What Cholo's story shows is that community engagement doesn't require a press release. It requires showing up.

Pit Bull Adoption: Fighting the Stigma That Gets Dogs Killed

Here's the part most outlets skip.

Cholo is a pit bull mix. So is Gojo. And that matters, because pit bulls make up a disproportionately large share of the overcrowded shelter population nationwide, largely due to breed misconceptions that drive higher rates of abandonment and lower rates of adoption. Kennel to Couch

The stigma is real, and it's costing lives. But Cholo spent his rescue day proving it wrong at every turn. He was calm at the grooming salon. He was gentle at the drive-through. He curled up in the back seat and let someone pat his back for the first time in who knows how long. The dog that made people cross the street on paper was, in reality, the dog who got an employee to come outside with a hamburger patty because she couldn't help herself.

That gap between perception and reality is where rescue advocates do their most important work. And no one in Dallas has done more of that work, at scale, than Tommy Habeeb.

Tommy Habeeb and "To The Rescue": What One Man With a Platform Can Do

When most people hear the name Tommy Habeeb, they think of "Cheaters," the long-running reality series he created and hosted starting in 2000. Habeeb has built a career spanning over four decades in entertainment, producing and hosting numerous television programs across lifestyle, adventure, and social issues. Grokipedia

But what he built next is what matters here.

In October 2020, Habeeb launched "To The Rescue," a half-hour weekly syndicated docu-series airing in over 200 markets nationwide. Each episode follows Habeeb across the United States as he documents how animal rescues and sanctuaries operate, against often impossible odds, to save dogs from abuse, neglect, behavioral issues, and medical crises. PR NewswireIMDb

The show's scope is intentionally wide: it intertwines the work of animal rescue organizations, municipal shelters, transporters, behaviorists, and foster families to reveal what it actually takes to get a dog from a kill list to a forever home. One episode took viewers inside CAMO, Canines Assisting Military Operators, a Palm Beach Gardens nonprofit that rescues shelter dogs and trains them as service animals for disabled veterans at no cost. That's the kind of cross-mission rescue work that changes two lives at once. Mynewstouse

Habeeb founded the nonprofit Forever Family Rescue Foundation to extend the show's reach beyond what a weekly episode can accomplish. As he put it: "We can only tell so many stories and save so many dogs on our show, but with the foundation, we can touch thousands more." Jejune Magazine

The foundation's stated mission is to help partner shelters achieve a 100% live release rate and ensure live adoptions across the country by finding forever homes for the most at-risk dogs. GuideStar

A hundred percent live release rate. That's not a feel-good goal. That's an operational standard most shelters can't come close to reaching without outside advocacy, funding, and visibility. Habeeb built the infrastructure to provide all three.

His motto? "Kindness, honesty, and not sweatin' the small stuff." For a man spending his career fighting a system that kills a million adoptable animals a year, that kind of steadiness is harder to maintain than it sounds. Jejune Magazine

What Happens When Strangers Show Up: The Human Stakes

Back in Dallas, the photos from Cholo's rescue day went up on Instagram. A dog playing with toys in an office. A dog who'd just had a hamburger and a bath and a car ride. A dog who had, by all measurable standards, the best day of his life while simultaneously being hours from his last.

It worked.

The morning after, Dallas Animal Services confirmed Cholo had gone home with a foster family committed to caring for him until a permanent placement was found. Two dogs who had almost run out of time found something else instead.

That outcome didn't come from a government program. It came from a reporter who showed up, a groomer who pitched in, a drive-through employee who brought out a burger, and a TikTok follower who recognized a dog's face from a phone screen and drove to the shelter.

Shelters that have gone public with urgent pleas for help have seen genuine outpourings of community response, though, as one shelter director noted, "pleading for help is not a sustainable solution alone." Humane World for Animals

That's exactly right. Viral moments save individual dogs. Systems save populations. The country needs both, and right now, it has too little of either.

What Happens Next: The Shelter Crisis Isn't Going Away

Cholo and Gojo got their second chance. Thousands of dogs in shelters across Dallas, across Texas, across the country won't.

Approximately one million pit bulls are euthanized annually in the United States, a direct result of overcrowded shelters and persistent breed bias. That number isn't driven by viciousness. It's driven by math, misconceptions, and a lack of available foster and adoptive homes. Kennel to Couch

The solutions aren't complicated, but they require buy-in: fostering, adopting, volunteering, sharing urgent placement posts on social media, and supporting organizations like Forever Family Rescue Foundation that are doing the systemic work municipal budgets can't cover.

Tommy Habeeb's "To The Rescue" has aired in over 200 markets and reached millions of viewers precisely because it shows the machinery behind the rescue, not just the happy ending. That transparency matters. It turns passive viewers into active participants. It shows people what "fostering a dog" actually looks like for a few days, a few weeks, sometimes a few months, and makes it feel less daunting.

DAS's own leadership has called on the community for adoptions, foster homes, volunteers, and reunifications, framing the ask as urgent and immediate, not someday. The city is asking. The question is who shows up. WFAA

Conclusion

The shelter dog rescue story of Cholo and Gojo isn't a feel-good distraction. It's a window into a system under enormous strain, held together by the kindness of strangers and the grit of advocates who refuse to look away. Tommy Habeeb built a television show and a foundation around that refusal, and it's reaching millions of people who didn't know they could make a difference until someone showed them how. If you're in Dallas or anywhere in this country, the animals at your local shelter aren't waiting for a policy fix. They're waiting for you. Visit totherescuetv.com to learn more, find your local rescue network, and make Cholo's kind of day possible for a dog who hasn't had one yet.

FAST FACTS

  • Dallas Animal Services reported 674 dogs housed in just 388 kennels in April 2026, the shelter's highest dog capacity in years. National Today
  • U.S. animal shelters are caring for 245,000 more companion animals in 2025 than they were in 2022. Humane World for Animals
  • "To The Rescue," hosted by Tommy Habeeb, airs in over 200 markets nationwide and premiered on October 17, 2020. PR Newswire
  • Approximately one million pit bulls are euthanized annually in the United States, driven primarily by shelter overcrowding and breed bias. Kennel to Couch
  • Operation Kindness transferred 852 animals out of Dallas Animal Services over a 12-month period, making it DAS's top transfer partner. Operation Kindness
  • Forever Family Rescue Foundation, founded by Tommy Habeeb and based in Dallas, TX, operates with a mission of achieving a 100% live release rate for partner shelters. GuideStar
  • Dallas Animal Services had 61 dogs on "Code Red" status, meaning they faced the most urgent risk of euthanasia, as of March 2024 during a standard operational period. The Dallas Express
  • Tommy Habeeb has produced over 100 episodes of "To The Rescue" as showrunner, executive producer, writer, and host. Grokipedia

FAQ

Q: What is a shelter dog rescue story and why do these cases go viral? A: A shelter dog rescue story typically involves a dog on an urgent placement or euthanasia list getting a last-minute reprieve through community action, foster placement, or adoption. They go viral because they're both heartbreaking and hopeful, combining a clear threat with an achievable resolution. Social media platforms amplify these cases in hours, often generating the public response that saves the animal's life.

Q: How bad is the Dallas Animal Services overcrowding crisis? A: As of April 2026, Dallas Animal Services housed 674 dogs in kennels designed for 388, making it one of the most overcrowded periods in the shelter's history. The facility has called on the community for urgent fosters, adopters, and volunteers, and has partnered with organizations including Operation Kindness to transfer animals out. The problem is part of a nationwide surge, with shelters collectively caring for 245,000 more animals than in 2022.

Q: Are pit bulls harder to get adopted from shelters? A: Yes, significantly. Pit bulls are euthanized at higher rates than most other breeds due to persistent breed misconceptions and, in some municipalities, breed-specific legislation. Despite evidence that individual temperament varies widely, pit bull mixes consistently make up a large share of shelter overcrowding populations and face lower adoption rates, which is why advocacy groups focus specifically on breed-neutral policies and public education.

Q: Who is Tommy Habeeb and what is "To The Rescue"? A: Tommy Habeeb is a veteran TV producer and host best known for creating "Cheaters." In 2020, he launched "To The Rescue," a nationally syndicated docu-series airing in over 200 markets that follows rescue dogs and the organizations saving them. He also founded Forever Family Rescue Foundation, a Dallas-based nonprofit working toward 100% live release rates at partner shelters. Learn more at totherescuetv.com.

Q: What can I do to help Dallas Animal Services right now? A: DAS actively offers same-day fostering, where you can walk in and take a dog home with short or long-term commitment. You can also adopt directly, volunteer onsite, share urgent placement posts on social media, or donate to transfer partners like Operation Kindness. Organizations like Forever Family Rescue Foundation (foreverfamilyrescue.org) and Tommy Habeeb's To The Rescue network (totherescuetv.com) also connect donors and volunteers to at-risk animals nationwide.

PHOTOS: Mackenzie Capp

CALL TO ACTION

Stucci Media exists because somebody has to tell the stories the rest of the media sanitizes, skips, or spins. Cholo's story is one of them. If you want reporting that connects the dots between the headlines and the humans behind them, you're in the right place. Subscribe below and get the truth delivered straight.

item.title: Venezuela Doublet Earthquake: Inside the Disaster That May Kill Thousands
item.dc:creator: roccistucci
item.content:encoded:
Venezuela doublet earthquake: At least 589 people have been confirmed dead and 2,980 injured following the most destructive earthquake sequence to strike Venezuela in more than a century — and seismologists, emergency planners, and the government's own acting president all say that number is almost certainly going to climb. On June 24, 2026, a magnitude 7.2 foreshock and a magnitude 7.5 mainshock struck Venezuela's north-central region 39 seconds apart, both at shallow depths of roughly 10 to 22 kilometers below the surface. Two quakes. Thirty-nine seconds. A nation shattered. NPRpaho

What Is a Doublet Earthquake — And Why Is It So Deadly?

Most people understand earthquakes as a single violent event followed by progressively smaller aftershocks. A doublet breaks that pattern entirely.

A seismic doublet occurs when two earthquakes of very similar magnitude take place very close together in time and very close together in space. The key distinction lies in that similarity of magnitudes: whereas a conventional aftershock is, under what is known as Båth's Law, roughly 1.2 magnitude units smaller than the main event, in a doublet both quakes share comparable strength — generally within about 0.4 units on the moment magnitude scale. euronews

The USGS has described the Venezuela pair as a doublet sequence, a phenomenon in which two tremors of similar magnitude strike roughly the same area at around the same time. The doublet pattern took place on a tangled system of faults near San Felipe, Venezuela — a zone so complex that it will take more time for researchers to understand precisely which faults within it ruptured. NBC News

Doublets are deadlier than single quakes because structurally compromised buildings collapse in the second event. The sequence creates a window of maximum danger for first responders that a single earthquake simply does not produce. Buildings that crack and lean during the 7.2 — but don't fall — are primed to collapse when the 7.5 arrives seconds later. There is no gap. There is no warning. There is no time. Outlook India

A previous doublet — of magnitudes 6.2 and 6.3 — struck an area west of Caracas in September 2025, killing at least one person and injuring more than 100 others. That was a warning. Wednesday's sequence was of a categorically different scale. Phys.org

The Fault System Beneath Venezuela's Feet

Venezuela's seismic risk is not a secret — it is simply underappreciated outside the region.

The doublet occurred along the diffuse onshore boundary between the Caribbean and South American tectonic plates. In northern Venezuela, these plates slide past each other at a rate of about 20 millimeters per year as the Caribbean Plate moves east relative to the South American Plate. This produces large strike-slip faults, including the Boconó, San Sebastián, and El Pilar fault systems — an active plate boundary that generates frequent shallow earthquakes, some of which can be damaging. The Conversation

The mainshock is the largest earthquake in Venezuela since the 1900 San Narciso earthquake, a magnitude 7.7 event that struck northeast of Caracas. The 1967 Caracas quake — far smaller at magnitude 6.5 — killed approximately 272 people, primarily in building collapses, and triggered the introduction of formal seismic construction codes in Venezuela. Those codes were a start. But decades of economic contraction eroded their impact. WikipediaThe Global Statistics

Venezuela does not have an early earthquake warning system — the kind that relies on sensors to detect the first waves of a quake and alert populations seconds before strong shaking arrives. "It's very distressing that there was basically no time to evacuate," one seismologist noted. That observation doesn't need much elaboration. PBS

The shaking is also followed by months or years of elevated landslide risk, because the rocks have been displaced. The next rainstorm in Venezuela will likely trigger landslides — meaning more damage and perhaps more deaths are still ahead. theconversation

How Venezuela's Crisis Turned a Disaster Into a Catastrophe

The geology explains the shaking. The politics explain the death toll.

About half of Caracas's five million residents are thought to live in informal housing — densely populated barrios comprising self-constructed structures built with unreinforced cinderblocks or bricks, often without formal foundations or steel reinforcement, mostly on mountainous hillsides surrounding the capital. These buildings were not designed to absorb seismic energy. They absorbed it anyway, and they collapsed. Al Jazeera

About 80 percent of Venezuela's population lives in quake-prone areas, and many live in houses not built to withstand strong earthquakes. Some of Caracas's hardest-hit neighborhoods are built on soft sediments that amplify seismic waves, making buildings more vulnerable to collapse than those constructed on solid bedrock. Al Jazeera

Rodríguez has only recently begun efforts to revive growth, with public services buckling under strain, hospitals short of equipment and medication, and frequent power outages — leaving emergency response stretched thin even before the quakes struck. NPR

Overwhelmed hospitals were forced to set up improvised wards in hallways and even on the street. Venezuela's health system has been undergoing a long crisis due to years of deterioration and lack of investment. CNN

With emergency resources stretched thin, volunteers arrived at disaster sites carrying their own shovels, hammers and basic tools to assist rescue efforts. Volunteer Sebastian Arias moved between neighborhoods where buildings had collapsed and found some sites overcrowded with helpers while others appeared to lack help and equipment entirely. That is not an emergency response system. That is improvisation in the face of institutional collapse. NPR

According to the CEPR, the US-based Center for Economic and Policy Research called on the United States and other governments to lift economic sanctions on Venezuela to allow aid to reach those in need more quickly, arguing that the government must be free to receive and allocate earthquake relief without restriction.

USGS PAGER: What the Death Toll Models Are Saying

The official confirmed death toll is 589. The statistical models suggest this number may be a fraction of the final count.

The USGS PAGER system — Prompt Assessment of Global Earthquakes for Response — estimated a 39% probability of between 1,000 and 10,000 deaths and a 37% probability of 10,000 to 100,000 deaths for the magnitude 7.5 mainshock alone. There is also an 11% probability that the final death toll will exceed 100,000. Wikipedia

PAGER combines earthquake shaking, population exposure, and country-specific vulnerability to estimate likely human and economic impact. For the magnitude 7.5 event, the USGS issued a red alert — a designation it applies globally only once or twice per year. Its model estimated approximately 7.75 million people exposed to moderate or stronger shaking, including 2.37 million at MMI VII intensity and 400,000 at MMI VIII. Miyamotointernational

Economic losses were projected at a 39% probability of falling between $10 billion and $100 billion — with upper estimates approaching 20% of Venezuela's entire GDP. Miyamotointernational

These are not predictions of what will happen. They are planning tools built from decades of global earthquake data applied to Venezuela's specific conditions. Venezuela scores poorly on nearly every dimension relevant to seismic resilience: building vulnerability, population density in high-risk zones, ground conditions, and economic capacity to mount an effective response. The PAGER system's models reflect that reality. The Global Statistics

The USGS PAGER alert for the June 24, 2026 Venezuela mainshock is publicly available and updated as field data comes in.

What International Aid Is — and Isn't — Doing

The global response has been fast. Whether it will be sufficient is a different question.

The US pledged $150 million in emergency aid — a $100 million contribution to a UN humanitarian fund and $50 million to aid organizations already in Venezuela — while deploying two elite urban search and rescue teams from Fairfax County, Virginia (80 personnel, 6 dogs) and Los Angeles County (71 personnel, 6 dogs). CNN

Search and rescue efforts are described as "very difficult" — potentially taking 12 to 48 hours to safely rescue a single person, according to a battalion chief from Fairfax County's special operations division. The variation of structures and situations is what complicates the effort. CNN

Secretary Rubio confirmed the teams draw on expertise in rescue operations, emergency medicine, engineering, and hazardous material management. Notably, the Fairfax team had participated in a strategic airlift exercise at Dover Air Force Base just days before the disaster, validating cache-loading procedures for sudden onset deployments. Council on Foreign Relations

Mexico, Chile, and El Salvador are sending emergency teams and medical supplies. The United States has also confirmed aerial imagery support to assess damage in remote coastal areas. NPR

There is a diplomatic undercurrent running beneath all of it. The international response is unfolding against a sensitive backdrop: former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro was seized in January during a US operation, further straining already tense relations between Washington and Caracas. That tension has not stopped cooperation — acting President Rodríguez confirmed that US officials had been in constant contact with her administration since the earthquakes struck, stating: "Venezuela will never forget the hand extended to our people in these hard hours." NPRHNGN

But there are structural limits to what speed of arrival can fix. Simón Bolívar International Airport is currently closed due to severe damage to its infrastructure — complicating the deployment of heavy equipment and personnel by air. The 2023 Türkiye-Syria doublet — which killed more than 56,000 people — exposed recurring failures in international disaster response: poor coordination among arriving teams, bottlenecks in transport corridors, and local organizations consistently sidelined in relief architecture. Venezuela's civil society, which has long filled gaps left by the state, is already doing the same work here. Whether the formal international response will learn from that history, or repeat it, is one of the central questions of the coming weeks. NBC NewsCGTN

According to the Pan American Health Organization, 21 regional and international Emergency Medical Teams from 15 countries have been identified, including three teams ready to deploy. PAHO is supporting rapid assessments of health facility functionality and identifying priority needs for medicines, medical supplies, oxygen, and fuel. paho

A Century of Warnings: Venezuela's Seismic History

Venezuela is not a country that has been blindsided by seismic risk. It is a country that could not afford to address it.

An estimated 30,000 people were killed in 1812 when a powerful earthquake devastated the cities of Mérida and Caracas — one of the most lethal natural disasters in the Western Hemisphere's recorded history. The 1812 quake struck along the same Boconó fault system that runs the length of the Venezuelan Andes for roughly 300 miles. The Caribbean plate has not stopped moving since then. It will not stop after this. Al Jazeera

Buildings constructed to post-1967 code standards performed significantly better in the 2026 event than older stock. But decades of economic contraction under the Maduro government and the broader humanitarian crisis meant that a large proportion of Venezuelan housing — including informal settlements covering significant portions of Caracas's hillsides and La Guaira's waterfront — was built outside code compliance. The Global Statistics

The European Commission had identified 7.9 million Venezuelans in need of humanitarian assistance before this disaster, with 56% living in extreme poverty. The earthquake did not create that fragility. It exposed it. CGTN

FAQ: Venezuela Earthquake 2026

What caused the Venezuela earthquakes on June 24, 2026?

The earthquakes occurred along the boundary between the Caribbean and South American tectonic plates, where the plates slide past each other at about 20 millimeters per year. This produces large strike-slip faults — including the Boconó, San Sebastián, and El Pilar fault systems — which have generated significant earthquakes throughout Venezuela's history. The Conversation

What is a doublet earthquake?

A seismic doublet occurs when two earthquakes of very similar magnitude strike very close together in time and location. Unlike a standard aftershock, which is typically 1.2 magnitude units smaller than the main event under Båth's Law, the two quakes in a doublet share comparable strength — generally within 0.4 units on the moment magnitude scale. euronews

How many people died in the Venezuela earthquake?

As of June 26, 2026, acting President Delcy Rodríguez confirmed 589 people dead and 2,980 injured. The death toll is expected to rise significantly. The USGS PAGER system has assigned a 37% probability that the final death toll will fall between 10,000 and 100,000, and an 11% probability it will exceed 100,000. NPRWikipedia

Why did so many buildings collapse in Venezuela?

About half of Caracas's population lives in informal housing built with unreinforced cinderblocks or bricks, often without formal foundations or steel reinforcement, mostly on hillsides surrounding the capital. Some of the hardest-hit neighborhoods are built on soft sediments that amplify seismic waves. Years of economic collapse also deferred maintenance on formal building stock that was already aging. Al JazeeraAl Jazeera

What international aid is being sent to Venezuela?

The United States pledged $150 million in emergency aid and deployed search and rescue teams from Fairfax County, Virginia (80 personnel) and Los Angeles County (71 personnel). Mexico, Chile, and El Salvador have also dispatched emergency teams and medical supplies. The United Nations is coordinating the deployment of additional urban search and rescue teams. CNNNPR

Is Venezuela at risk of more earthquakes after this?

The USGS assessed a 99% chance of at least one magnitude 4 aftershock hitting Venezuela within the following week, and a 24% chance of a magnitude 6 or larger event occurring. Beyond aftershocks, the region also faces elevated landslide risk for months or years, because the earthquake has displaced rocks across hillside terrain — meaning future rainstorms could trigger additional casualties. PBStheconversation

What Comes Next

The 72-hour window most likely to yield living survivors is closing. After that, the mission changes — from rescue to recovery, from recovery to reconstruction. For Venezuela, reconstruction means rebuilding not just buildings but the institutional capacity that determines whether the next earthquake kills hundreds or thousands.

The USGS warned immediately after the quake that "high casualties and extensive damage are probable, and the disaster is likely widespread." That language was calibrated. It was also correct. The confirmed death toll will likely look like an undercount within days, as rescue teams reach isolated coastal communities and the full scope of La Guaira's destruction is systematically mapped. Al Jazeera

Disaster mortality in least developed countries runs 2.5 times higher than the global average, according to the UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction. The earthquake did not create Venezuela's fragility — it exposed structural underinvestment that is neither unique nor inevitable. CGTN

What is unique is the scale. The June 24, 2026 mainshock is the largest earthquake in Venezuela since 1900. Everyone who was alive for the 1967 quake — the previous benchmark — has now lived through something measurably worse. The people digging through rubble with their own shovels in Caracas and La Guaira understand that better than any model can capture. Wikipedia

Follow Stucci Media's continuing coverage of the Venezuela earthquake relief effort](INTERNAL LINK: Venezuela earthquake coverage hub) as the situation develops.

item.title: West Bank Is Burning. Even Israel's Military Says So.
item.dc:creator: roccistucci
item.content:encoded:
Israeli settler violence in the West Bank is now running at roughly six attacks per day in 2026, according to the United Nations — and the most alarming condemnations aren't coming from Palestinian spokespeople or European capitals. They're coming from inside Israel's own military. That detail changes the entire frame of this story, and most of the media covering it has missed it completely.

Background and Context

The West Bank has never been a quiet place. But what's happening in 2026 is different in scale, frequency, and official acknowledgment. UN experts warned in June 2026 that settler brutality has reached unprecedented levels, with at least thirteen Palestinians killed and close to five hundred injured in just the first five months of the year — outpacing figures from every prior year on record. United Nations

The attacks follow a pattern that security analysts describe as coordinated rather than spontaneous. Since Israel's far-right government took office in December 2022, over 4,500 settler attacks have been recorded — roughly four per day — resulting in the complete depopulation of 59 Palestinian communities and the displacement of more than 5,500 people. In 2026, that pace accelerated sharply. J Street

Three U.S. citizens are among the civilians killed by settlers in that period, according to J Street's analysis of the data, with none of those deaths resulting in criminal charges.

What Israeli Settler Violence in the West Bank Looks Like in 2026

This isn't stone-throwing at checkpoints. Settlers stormed the village of Fandaqumiya and the town of Seilat al-Dahr in a weekend rampage that lasted more than six hours, struck over 14 villages, attacked dozens of Palestinians, and, by the account of one Israeli opposition figure, went completely unchecked. Time

In March 2026, settlers broke into a Bedouin family home in Khirbet Humsa, attacked residents including children, stole valuables and livestock, and sexually assaulted a man. During the Eid holiday, mobs torched vehicles, hurled Molotov cocktails at occupied homes, and spraypainted death threats on walls in Arabic-speaking towns. Arab Center DC

Israeli prosecutors did charge six settlers — five of them minors — after a mosque attack, with charges including arson under terrorist circumstances and racially-motivated assault. That prosecution made news precisely because it's rare. Upwards of 96 percent of settler violence incidents never result in formal charges being filed. Al JazeeraJ Street

Settler Attacks Are a Strategy, Not a Fringe Problem

The harder truth that most Western coverage sidesteps: this violence isn't fringe behavior that Israel's government is failing to suppress. According to multiple analysts, it functions as policy.

Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has unveiled a plan that would annex 82 percent of the West Bank and has repeatedly called for "encouraging the emigration" of Palestinians — a thinly veiled phrase for forced displacement. The logic is brutally linear: remove the people, then legalize the land. J Street

The IDF has actively helped settlers establish outposts, coordinating their timing and location and deploying forces to guard them. Those outposts then serve as launching points for attacks on neighboring Palestinian communities. The institution tasked with protecting civilians in the West Bank has been, in documented cases, helping to install the people attacking them. J Street

In April 2026, the Israeli government authorized construction of 34 new settlements in the West Bank — nearly six times the number approved across the thirty years following the 1993 Oslo Accords. Settlement construction and settler violence aren't parallel phenomena. They move together. Arab Center DC

The IDF Speaks Up — and Gets Ignored

Here's where the story breaks from the standard Western media frame. IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir visited the West Bank specifically to address the surge in settler violence, warning officers that "a threatening minority from within" is endangering Israel's security and its values. CSMonitor.com

That's the appointed head of Israel's military calling settlers a domestic security threat. It didn't get the headline it deserved.

IDF Central Command head Maj. Gen. Avi Bluth issued an open letter urging rabbis, parents, educators, and public leaders to speak out in a "clear voice," warning that if the situation continued, it risked igniting a new front in the West Bank. A retired Israeli general, Israel Ziv, was blunt about why those warnings may not land: without political condemnation from the government, it will be "very hard" for the army to do its job. CSMonitor.com

Secretary of State Marco Rubio expressed public concern, and analysts credit U.S. pressure with producing a wave of rare condemnations from senior Israeli officials who typically dismiss settler violence as marginal. One of Israel's most influential commentators stated on television that there's "no question it's terror." That's new. Whether it changes anything on the ground remains an open question. NPR

The Human Toll — What Displacement Actually Means

Statistics can numb. The individual cases don't.

In May 2026, settlers exhumed a deceased Palestinian man — an act that further intensified international criticism of settler violence. In March, during a multi-day rampage following the death of an Israeli settler in an ATV accident, Palestinian families across the Nablus region watched their cars burn and their windows shatter while holding children inside. Wikipedia

Nearly 700 Palestinians in nine communities were displaced due to settler attacks in the first months of 2026 alone, and more than 1,000 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli troops and settlers in the West Bank since October 2023. Time

One Palestinian father, who watched his son killed by settlers, switched to Hebrew mid-interview with NPR specifically to reach an Israeli audience. "The Jews are afraid to put this on Israeli television," he said. "The whole world needs to see this." NPR

What the Data Shows — and What Accountability Looks Like

The accountability gap in the West Bank is structural, not incidental. Israeli law enforcement investigations of settler attacks are grossly inadequate — Palestinians are often fearful of retribution if they report incidents, and the location of police stations inside Israeli settlements makes it nearly impossible for Palestinians to access them. Al-Haq

In September 2025, the European Commission proposed suspending Israel's preferential trade access. Canada imposed four rounds of sanctions on individual settlers since May 2024. The UK, Australia, New Zealand, and Norway jointly sanctioned Israeli ministers Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in June 2025. The Century Foundation

The U.S. position is more complicated. On his first day in office, President Trump rescinded the Biden-era executive order that had barred Americans from dealing with Israeli settlers and entities accused of involvement in Palestinian violence. Within hours of that announcement, a new settler rampage hit the northern West Bank village of Al-Funduq. NBC News

Analysts at the Atlantic Council have argued that the Trump administration actually has unique political leverage here — and that designating extremist settler organizations as terrorist entities would simultaneously weaken Hamas's political prospects, which benefit every time Palestinian civilians are attacked without consequence.

What Comes Next for West Bank Settlers and U.S. Policy

Israel is approaching a general election in fall 2026, and most viable challengers to Prime Minister Netanyahu lean right, viewing the cementing of West Bank gains as an imperative. Netanyahu, managing a fractious far-right coalition, has strong incentive to keep the settler constituency satisfied rather than prosecute it. Washington Examiner

That creates a pressure point for Washington. The Abraham Accords — Trump's signature foreign policy achievement — depend on Arab states believing the U.S. can play an honest broker role. Extremist settler violence imperils broader regional progress, including Trump's own efforts to preserve the ceasefire in Gaza and expand the Abraham Accords. Atlantic Council

For Americans who care about rule of law, about the credibility of U.S. alliances, and about the long-term stability of a region where American lives and treasure have been committed for decades, the West Bank in 2026 is a test. Not of loyalty to Israel, but of seriousness about the principles that make that alliance worth defending.

Conclusion

Israeli settler violence in the West Bank has reached a scale that the IDF's own leadership describes as a threat to Israel's security and values. Six attacks per day. Thirteen Palestinians killed in five months. Ninety-six percent of incidents never charged. The facts aren't contested — they're documented by the UN, the Israeli military, and multiple allied governments now imposing sanctions. What's contested is the political will to treat those facts as a problem. For Americans, the question isn't whether to stand with Israel. It's whether standing with Israel means looking away while its own generals are sounding the alarm.

FAST FACTS

  • Israeli settler attacks in the West Bank rose to approximately six per day in 2026, according to the United Nations. Al Jazeera
  • At least 13 Palestinians were killed and nearly 500 injured by settlers in just the first five months of 2026, surpassing figures from prior years. United Nations
  • More than 4,500 settler attacks have been recorded since Israel's far-right government took office in December 2022, forcibly depopulating 59 Palestinian communities. J Street
  • Upwards of 96 percent of settler violence incidents never result in criminal charges, according to rights group analysis. J Street
  • Israel authorized construction of 34 new West Bank settlements in April 2026 — nearly six times the number approved across the 30 years following Oslo. Arab Center DC
  • The UK, Canada, France, and Norway coordinated sanctions in June 2026 against Israeli settlers and organizations enabling West Bank violence. Steptoe
  • President Trump rescinded Biden-era settler sanctions on his first day in office; hours later, a new settler rampage struck Al-Funduq in the West Bank. NBC News
  • More than 1,000 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli troops and settlers in the West Bank since October 2023. Time

FAQ

Q: What is Israeli settler violence in the West Bank? A: Israeli settler violence refers to attacks by Israeli civilians living in the occupied West Bank against Palestinian residents and their property. These attacks include arson, armed assaults, livestock theft, property destruction, and killings. The UN recorded approximately six such attacks per day in 2026. Most incidents result in no criminal charges, and Israeli government critics argue the violence is enabled by political leadership that opposes accountability for settlers.

Q: How many Palestinians have been displaced by settler attacks in 2026? A: According to the United Nations, nearly 700 Palestinians across nine communities were displaced by settler attacks in the early months of 2026 alone. Since October 2023, more than 5,500 Palestinians have been displaced from 59 communities due to sustained settler violence. Displacement is driven by arson, armed intimidation, and attacks on essential infrastructure including water and agriculture.

Q: What is the U.S. government's current policy on West Bank settler violence? A: President Trump revoked Biden-era sanctions on violent West Bank settlers on his first day in office in January 2025. The U.S. no longer explicitly backs a two-state solution. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has expressed concern about the violence, and U.S. pressure contributed to rare public condemnations by senior Israeli officials, but no formal sanctions have been reimposed. Allied nations including the UK, Canada, France, and Norway imposed coordinated sanctions in June 2026.

Q: Has Israel's own military condemned settler violence? A: Yes. IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir publicly warned that a "threatening minority from within" was endangering Israel's security and values. Central Command head Maj. Gen. Avi Bluth issued an open letter calling on Israeli civil society to speak out. Prominent Israeli commentators have used the term "Jewish terrorism" on national television — a phrase that was previously taboo in mainstream Israeli discourse.

Q: Are Israeli settlers legally allowed to live in the West Bank? A: Under international law, Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are considered illegal by most countries and international bodies, including the United Nations. Israel disputes this characterization. More than 500,000 Israeli citizens currently live in West Bank settlements and outposts. Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has stated his goal is to annex 82 percent of the West Bank and has called settlement expansion "Zionism at its best."

CALL TO ACTION

Most outlets covering this story either cheerlead one side or bury the parts that don't fit their frame. At Stucci Media, we follow the facts wherever they lead — because that's the only kind of journalism worth your time. If you want the West Bank story, the Iran story, and every other story that the cable networks are too cautious or too captured to tell straight, you know where to find us. Subscribe, and never get spun again.

item.title: The 149-Year Family Farm That Just Became Missouri's Best-Kept Wedding Secret
item.dc:creator: roccistucci
item.content:encoded:
The best wedding venue in Cabool, Missouri wasn't built by a developer, designed by a consultant, or funded by a private equity rollup. It was built by a father who wanted his daughter to have the most beautiful wedding day imaginable, on land his family has farmed for nearly 150 years. That's the whole story. And somehow, that's exactly why it works.

The Creek sits at 5530 Highway Z in Cabool, Missouri, deep in the heart of Texas County, atop the Ozark Plateau. Cabool was established in 1882 along the route of the Kansas City, Fort Scott, and Memphis Railroad, and has served as a vital commercial and service center for the surrounding Ozark region for well over a century. This is not a manufactured tourist destination. It's a working American town with deep roots, surrounded by rugged hills, springs, creeks, and rivers, with a community spirit that longtime residents describe as some of the friendliest and most caring people in the country. GrokipediaTexascountymissouri

The Amick family has been part of that community since 1877. Their farm, handed down through generations in the Hamilton Creek Valley, became the foundation for something Oliver and Andrea Amick never originally planned to build at all. The Creek was born as a gift: a one-of-a-kind ceremony space created so their daughter could have the wedding of her dreams on land that carries the weight of a family's entire history. When word got out about what they'd built, the response was immediate. People wanted in.

The Wedding Venue Cabool Missouri Didn't Know It Needed

Central Missouri couples planning weddings have historically faced a familiar frustration: their choices are either the polished, pricey venues clustered around Branson and Springfield, or they settle for generic banquet halls that carry no soul and tell no story. The natural beauty of the Ozarks has long attracted soon-to-be newlyweds to the area, but nearly all of the editorial coverage, venue directories, and regional guides have focused on the southwest corner of the state, leaving the Texas County corridor functionally invisible to engaged couples searching for something real. 417mag

The Creek fills that gap with force.

Set in the Hamilton Creek Valley, the venue offers outdoor ceremony spaces built directly alongside the water, an indoor reception hall for those who want timeless elegance without the weather gamble, and views across the Ozark Plateau that no decorator and no budget can replicate. The bridal suite and groom's lounge give wedding parties dedicated space to get ready and gather before the moment. And because The Creek operates as a true DIY venue, couples rent the property and make it entirely their own. You bring your vision, your vendors, your people. The Amicks make sure you have the perfect setting to pull it off, and they're on hand throughout to help if anything comes up. What they don't do is get in the way. Your day runs the way you want it to run.

That combination of breathtaking natural setting and genuine flexibility is exactly what the market has been missing.

Ozark Plateau Event Center With 149 Years of American Story Behind It

Here's what separates The Creek from every competitor in a 100-mile radius: the land itself has been lived on, worked, and loved since 1877. Texas County, the largest of Missouri's 114 counties, comprises 1,179 square miles of Ozark Highland. Pioneers came to Texas County in the 1820s from Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee, and the Carolinas, homesteading fertile valleys and building small family farms that remain a major part of the landscape today. The Amick farm is part of that unbroken thread. Texascountymissouri

Cabool itself carries layers of legend. The city was named after Kabul, Afghanistan, using an older English spelling, by a railroad engineer in 1882 who thought the area of southern Texas County resembled the region he'd seen overseas. It remains the only "Cabool" in the United States. The town's name carries echoes of an explorer's wonder at a landscape so distinctive, so unlike anything else in the Midwest, that it reminded him of somewhere half a world away. Wikipedia

That landscape hasn't changed. The Hamilton Creek Valley still delivers that same sense of arrival, that feeling that you've found something most people drive past without ever knowing exists. Walking onto The Creek property is not a manufactured experience. It's the real Missouri Ozarks, offered to you by the family who has stewarded it for nearly a century and a half.

What the Competition Gets Wrong About Missouri Ozarks Weddings

The national wedding industry loves the word "rustic." Venues from coast to coast have perfected the art of charging premium prices for manufactured roughness, barn wood panels installed six months ago, Edison bulb strands from a wholesale supplier. That fake-rustic trend peaked, and couples know it. According to The Knot's 2025 Real Weddings Study, 72% of couples said the most important aspect of planning was that their guests were well taken care of and had a good time, not that the aesthetic hit a Pinterest board. The Knot

Beyond aesthetic fatigue, there's a cost problem. Full-service wedding venues in Missouri's competitive markets bundle coordination fees, mandatory catering minimums, and "preferred vendor" requirements that quietly double the final bill. For couples who want to hire their own caterer, bring their own flowers, and run their event the way they actually want to, those constraints aren't a feature. They're a dealbreaker.

The Creek takes a different approach. Rent the venue at a price point designed to keep costs manageable, bring in whoever and whatever makes your event yours, and celebrate without a checklist someone else wrote. The Amicks will be there if you need them. They simply trust their guests to know what they want.

The Creek doesn't need a designer to simulate authenticity. The authenticity is built into the soil. There's a difference between a venue made to look like it belongs to history, and a venue that actually does. Every couple who spends time at The Creek can feel it.

The Story Behind The Arch: When a Father Builds a Venue

There's a moment in every good origin story where you realize the thing being built wasn't really about business at all. For The Creek, that moment is the reason the arch exists.

Oliver and Andrea Amick didn't set out to open an event center. They set out to give their daughter the most beautiful wedding day they could imagine, on the land where their family has lived and worked for generations. What they built in the process, a ceremony space beside Hamilton Creek that captured the full natural beauty of the Ozark Plateau Valley, turned out to be something everyone who saw it wanted for themselves.

That's the kind of origin story money can't manufacture. It's the kind of story that makes families drive two hours from St. Louis, makes couples from Springfield and Kansas City put Cabool on their map for the first time. Word of mouth has always been the most powerful marketing channel in rural America, and the word on The Creek has been getting out fast.

The Amicks want to share their little piece of heaven. That's the entire pitch. There's no corporate mission statement, no brand pyramid, no "experiential hospitality" buzzword in the lobby. There is a family farm, a creek, and generations of stewardship, now yours to rent for the most important days of your life.

Why Flexible DIY Venues Win in 2026

The experiential event industry has been pointing in one direction for years. Couples want meaning and freedom, not a package someone else curated. Leading wedding industry voices have noted that couples increasingly want venues that accommodate guests from different backgrounds, create environments where people feel like themselves, and offer experiences that extend beyond the traditional format. A sprawling resort with a mandatory four-hour coordinator contract delivers a predictable experience; a 149-year family farm in the Missouri Ozarks where you set the rules delivers something you actually remember. The Knot

The DIY model also has real financial logic behind it. When couples aren't locked into venue-preferred vendors, mandatory catering minimums, or add-on fees for basic access, the savings are meaningful. They can hire the caterer their family loves, bring the florist they've worked with for years, and keep the money they'd otherwise spend on coordination fees inside their own budget.

For corporate clients, the case is equally compelling. Team-building retreats and business gatherings in cookie-cutter hotel conference rooms have a well-documented productivity problem: nobody's inspired by drop ceilings and a complimentary continental breakfast. Placing a leadership team in a setting like the Hamilton Creek Valley, away from screens, surrounded by genuine American countryside, changes the conversation. Bring your own agenda, your own catering, your own team-building structure. The Creek provides the backdrop. The rest is yours. The Ozarks have long been described by residents and visitors alike as some of the most beautiful and peaceful land in the country, and that environment does real work on human creativity and connection. Texascountymissouri

What Happens Next: The Creek and the Future of Rural Event Culture

Small-town America has a venue problem. Rural communities across the country are watching their young people drive an hour or two to find places to celebrate their most important life events, because nothing close to home measures up. The Creek is a direct answer to that dynamic in south central Missouri.

The ripple effects matter. When a wedding or reunion happens at The Creek, guests coming from Springfield, St. Louis, Kansas City, and beyond spend time in Cabool and Texas County. They stop at local businesses, experience a community they might never have visited otherwise, and leave with a different picture of rural Missouri than the one most people carry. A single successful event venue in a rural area can quietly reshape the economic and cultural energy of an entire region.

Texas County has always been home to people who are a different breed, with a community spirit and genuine care for their neighbors that residents and historians have noted for generations. The Creek fits that tradition perfectly. It's not a transplant or a development project. It grew organically from the soil of a family that loves this place and wants to share it. Texascountymissouri

Watch this venue. The word is spreading, the seasons are filling up, and the Missouri Ozarks event market is about to find out that its best-kept secret has been sitting in the Hamilton Creek Valley all along.

Conclusion

The wedding venue Cabool Missouri couples have been waiting for didn't come from a developer's spreadsheet. It came from a family's love for their land and their daughter, from 149 years of stewardship on the Ozark Plateau, and from Oliver and Andrea Amick's decision to open their ancestral home to the world. The Creek at 5530 Highway Z is more than an event space; it's proof that the most powerful things in this country are still built by families, not corporations. Rent the venue, bring your people, and make it yours. Whether you're planning a wedding along Hamilton Creek, a milestone birthday under Missouri skies, a family reunion in the Ozark hills, or a corporate retreat that actually gets results, The Creek is ready. The only question is whether you'll book before everyone else finds out.

FAST FACTS

  1. The Amick family farm has been the ancestral home of The Creek's founding family since 1877, making the property 149 years old.
  2. The Creek is located in Cabool, Missouri, the largest city in Texas County, Missouri's largest geographic county at 1,179 square miles.
  3. Cabool was named after Kabul, Afghanistan, using an older English spelling, by a railroad engineer in 1882 who found the southern Missouri Ozark landscape reminiscent of the region he had seen overseas. Wikipedia
  4. The Creek operates as a DIY rental venue: couples and event hosts rent the property, bring their own vendors and vision, and run their event their way, with the Amick family available on-site throughout.
  5. The venue serves weddings, birthdays, anniversaries, family and class reunions, and corporate business gatherings, making it central Missouri's most versatile and affordable private event destination.
  6. Texas County is the largest county by land area in the state of Missouri, yet remains almost entirely absent from major regional wedding venue directories, leaving The Creek positioned in a near-zero-competition event market. Grokipedia
  7. The Creek is located at 5530 Highway Z, Cabool, MO 65689, reachable via the intersection of U.S. Routes 60 and 63, the region's primary highway corridor.
  8. The venue was originally built by Oliver and Andrea Amick to host their daughter's wedding, then opened to the public after demand from everyone who saw it made the decision for them.

FAQ

Q: What is the best wedding venue in Cabool, Missouri? A: The Creek at 5530 Highway Z in Cabool, MO is the premier wedding venue in central Missouri's Texas County. Set on a family farm in the Hamilton Creek Valley atop the Ozark Plateau, it offers outdoor creekside ceremonies, a warm indoor reception hall, a bridal suite, and a groom's lounge. The Creek is a DIY rental venue, so couples bring their own vendors and run their day their way. Call (636) 777-0236 to inquire about availability.

Q: Is The Creek in Cabool MO a DIY venue? A: Yes. The Creek operates as a rental venue where couples and event hosts rent the property and handle their own coordination, vendors, and setup. The Amick family is present and available throughout every event to assist if needed, but the event belongs entirely to the guests. This model keeps costs significantly lower than full-service venues and gives couples complete creative freedom.

Q: How far is The Creek Cabool MO from Springfield or St. Louis? A: Cabool, Missouri sits approximately 77 miles east of Springfield via U.S. Route 60, making The Creek a practical destination for couples and guests from across southwest and central Missouri. For St. Louis guests, Cabool is accessible via I-44 and U.S. Route 63, positioning The Creek as a reachable Ozark destination for couples across the entire state.

Q: Is The Creek a family-owned venue? A: Yes. The Creek is owned and operated by Oliver and Andrea Amick, whose family has farmed the Hamilton Creek Valley land since 1877. The venue was originally created to host the Amick family's own daughter's wedding, then opened to the public. The family remains present at every event, available to assist, while allowing guests to run their celebration exactly as they choose.

Q: What makes The Creek different from other Ozark wedding venues? A: The Creek combines authentic 149-year family farm history with a true DIY rental model. Unlike commercial venues that require preferred vendors, mandatory coordination packages, or catering minimums, The Creek lets you rent the space and make it completely your own. The natural beauty of Hamilton Creek Valley on the Ozark Plateau requires no decoration to impress, and the Amick family's on-site presence means you're never on your own if something comes up.

CALL TO ACTION

If you want the news that actually matters, the American stories the major outlets overlook, and the facts they won't frame straight, Stucci Media is where you come. We don't chase clicks. We chase truth. Subscribe now and join the readers who expect more from their media than a headline designed to make them angry and a paywall designed to make them poorer.

item.title: JP Gauna Actor: The Choctaw Star Hollywood Waved In Off the Street
item.dc:creator: roccistucci
item.content:encoded:
He was crossing the street in Dallas when a television crew waved him over. JP Gauna, the JP Gauna actor now appearing on three major streaming platforms in the same calendar year, almost kept walking. Someone shoved a business card into his hand and told him to take a photo against a white wall and email it. He laughed. He did it anyway. Five minutes later, his phone rang. He had a role on Queen of the South before he had any idea what he was doing.

That is how careers start sometimes, not in some conservatory in New York or an MFA program in Los Angeles, but on a sidewalk in Texas, in a moment so ordinary it almost doesn't happen.

From the Choctaw Nation to the Queen of the South Set

Jeremy "JP" Gauna grew up in Texas with two things locked into him early: athletic discipline and work ethic. He was all-state in high school, a dual-sport college athlete, and eventually played semi-pro basketball in Oklahoma City. He is Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma and Mexican, and he carries both with him. His grandfather, Jimmy Lee Barkus, is the man he points to when the conversation turns to foundations. The lesson was practical and absolute: if you have a car, the distance to the job is not an excuse. You show up. You work.

"Choctaws are hard workers," Gauna has said, and he means it as both a cultural observation and a personal creed.

Before acting, he spent seven years in marketing and advertising at The Dallas Morning News. That is not a footnote. That is the whole first chapter. Seven years of corporate work, building skills, paying bills, and having zero reason to believe any of it would pivot into a television career. Then came that walk to work, that film crew, that hallway marked for actors.

Once he landed background work on Queen of the South, the veteran actor Zahn McClarnon, who has since become one of the most respected Indigenous voices on television, told him the truth plainly: if he was serious about this, he needed training. Gauna enrolled at R.E.A.C.T. Studio under instructor Michelle Sherrill. He used paid time off from the newspaper, burning vacation days to sit in acting classes. He eventually earned a small speaking role on Queen of the South, which got him an agent. Then COVID hit, and the newspaper career ended with a severance package and the encouragement of colleagues who saw something in him he was still learning to trust.

The pandemic that silenced everything else gave him his next opening. His friend Willie Molina called asking if he wanted to work as a production assistant on The Chosen. Gauna had no idea what the job entailed. He took it.

JP Gauna and the Weight of 1883

The Yellowstone universe found him first as a warrior, not a supporting character, not comic relief, not a Hollywood Indian in the tired, degraded sense of that phrase. In 1883, the sprawling Paramount+ prequel that introduced audiences to the Dutton family origins, Gauna played the Native warrior whose arrow ended the life of Elsa Dutton, played by Isabel May. It is the kind of role that defines a performance with one scene. He appeared in two episodes. He was unforgettable.

That role was not background noise. It was a pivot point in the entire series, the moment the show committed to refusing any version of history where westward expansion is a triumphant march. The first season of 1923 tracked the character of Teonna Rainwater as she escaped a brutal Indian assimilation boarding school run by the Catholic Church, and the larger Sheridan universe had been building Indigenous storylines with genuine weight for years. Gauna's warrior in 1883 was part of that architecture, a reminder that the land the Duttons claimed was already inhabited by people who would defend it. The Hollywood Reporter

He did not complain about the brevity of the role. He understood what it meant inside the story.

The Call Nobody Wanted to Make

What happened next requires context, and some care.

Cole Brings Plenty was found dead in Kansas at age 27 in April of 2024, months before filming of 1923 Season 2 began. He had been playing Pete Plenty Clouds in Season 1, and there was significant storyline still ahead for the character. His death was a blow to an entire cast and crew that had become something close to family. The Season 2 premiere honored him with an "In Memoriam" tribute, showing his photo before the first episode's story began. Just JaredJust Jared

The producers faced a choice: write Pete out, or find someone who could carry the character forward with integrity. They chose to continue the story, and they chose JP Gauna.

Gauna earned the approval of Cole Brings Plenty's family before accepting the role. That detail is not procedural. It is the whole moral weight of the decision compressed into a single act of respect. He did not take the job and announce himself. He went to the family first. MovieWeb

"It is a lot of weight on my shoulders, but I gladly wear it," Gauna said.

The two men had known each other personally, which made the assignment simultaneously easier and harder. Gauna has spoken publicly about their conversations, the daily check-ins, his friend's barely contained excitement about the upcoming season. "Cole had so much expectations with the character. He had so much joy knowing that he was getting to be a part of six episodes, and that was taken away from him abruptly," Gauna told The Hollywood Reporter. Collider

"Having that conversation with Taylor [Sheridan] at the beginning was very bittersweet," Gauna said. "I want to celebrate this opportunity, but I also want to grieve for my friend." Collider

That is not the language of an actor angling for a profile piece. That is a person holding two real things at once.

Gauna appeared in six episodes of 1923 Season 2 as Pete Plenty Clouds, and his co-star Aminah Nieves, who plays Teonna Rainwater, made clear that his connection to Cole was not a liability but a bridge. "Because Jeremy also knew Coco, that created an already established safe and protective space, and he honored Coco as best as he could. I think he's done a great job. It couldn't have been anyone else," Nieves said. The Hollywood Reporter

American Primeval and the Climb Nobody Covered

While the 1923 storyline generated most of the press around Gauna in early 2025, he had already delivered a full performance arc in another major production before Pete Plenty Clouds appeared on screen.

American Primeval, Netflix's six-episode limited series set during the Utah War of 1857, premiered January 9, 2025, to critical attention as an unflinching Western that dismantled the romanticized mythology of the American frontier. Gauna played Tall Shadow across five episodes, a substantial commitment in a show built around a strong ensemble cast that included Taylor Kitsch and Betty Gilpin. Rotten Tomatoes

Critics praised the series as a brutal and visually stunning production, calling it arguably the best TV series about the American West. Reviews pointed specifically to the show's commitment to honest Indigenous representation, the idea that Native people in this period were not background ornamentation but active, complex forces in the story of the frontier. Rotten Tomatoes

That is the kind of work Gauna has been quietly accumulating. Not the one-episode splash. The five-episode build. The six-episode arc. The steady presence that makes other actors lean on him for the emotional grounding of a scene.

Why These Stories? The Mission Behind the Work

There is a question worth asking any actor who takes on the roles Gauna gravitates toward. The boarding schools. The raids. The forced assimilation. The loss. Why keep choosing stories that sit inside the most painful chapters of American history?

His answer is direct: "You don't want to deal with it because it's too rough; it's too personal; it's too close to home. Those are the stories that I want to be a part of, the ones that make you feel uncomfortable and make you understand what really happened."

He has also said this, which should be printed on a wall somewhere: "Without these stories being told, history could repeat itself. And we definitely do not need to regress. We need to progress."

That is a conservative truth dressed in the language of Indigenous advocacy, because it is both. The belief that history must be known accurately, that forgetting is dangerous, that the past is not optional background reading, these are not partisan positions. They are responsible ones. A USC study examining the 1,600 top-grossing films between 2007 and 2022 found that fewer than 0.25% of all speaking roles went to Native American characters, with the percentage never exceeding 1% in any single year evaluated. In that context, every role Gauna takes is pushing against a documented scarcity, not a perceived one. Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma

He is also aware of what happens when the door opens. "I've been fortunate enough to walk and step through that door but then stick a boulder in the door to keep it open for others."

That is the work beyond the work.

What Comes Next: Drew's World and the Work Already Done

Gauna's IMDb page currently lists 14 acting credits spanning 2018 through 2025, with a pre-production project already in the pipeline. He will play Uncle Ray in Drew's World, adding yet another character to a growing body of work that now spans Netflix, Paramount+, network television, and independent film, including Terror on the Prairie, The Last Son, Far Haven, Birthright Outlaw, Cottonmouth (available on Prime Video), and The Harbinger.

He is also still the person who believes humor is a practical tool, not a retreat from hard subject matter. "If I can make one person smile a day, then I am doing something right." He has said he believes humor is one of the most underrated mechanisms for ending racism. That reads as a serious position, not a platitude.

The man who almost didn't cross the street is now one of the most consistently working Native actors in American television. He did not get here through a diversity mandate or a studio initiative. He got here because his grandfather taught him that distance is not an excuse, and because someone on a film crew waved him into a hallway, and because he went to acting class on his vacation days, and because when a friend died and left a role behind, he asked the family for permission before he said yes.

That is a story Hollywood rarely tells. StucciMedia is telling it.

The JP Gauna Standard: Truth, Identity, and the Long Game

The JP Gauna actor story is about more than credits and streaming platforms. It is about what happens when a person builds something real, brick by brick, without a shortcut in sight, and then uses the platform that comes from that discipline to say things that need saying.

A recent study found that television shows featuring authentic Native American representation significantly increase support for Indigenous issues and receive stronger critical and audience approval, which means what Gauna is doing on screen is measurably changing how audiences understand a portion of American history they were never taught properly. That is not a minor contribution. NCTA

He is 36, working at a pace most actors half his age cannot sustain, carrying the weight of a friend's unfinished role with grace, and keeping the door propped open for whoever is coming behind him.

The sidwalk in Dallas was just the beginning.

Fast Facts

  1. JP Gauna holds 14 acting credits spanning 2018 to 2025, with an additional project, Drew's World, currently in pre-production.
  2. He is a member of the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma and of Mexican heritage, representing both identities throughout his career.
  3. Before acting, Gauna spent seven years in marketing and advertising at The Dallas Morning News.
  4. He was cast in 1923 Season 2 with the blessing of Cole Brings Plenty's family, playing Pete Plenty Clouds across six episodes.
  5. His role as Tall Shadow in Netflix's American Primeval spanned five episodes of the acclaimed 2025 limited series.
  6. Native American characters have accounted for fewer than 0.25% of speaking roles in the top 1,600 grossing films between 2007 and 2022, per a USC study. Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma
  7. Gauna played the warrior who delivered the fatal arrow to Elsa Dutton in Taylor Sheridan's 1883, one of the most pivotal scenes in the Yellowstone universe.
  8. He was an all-state athlete in high school and a dual-sport college athlete who went on to play semi-pro basketball in Oklahoma City.

FAQ

Q: Who is JP Gauna the actor? A: JP Gauna, full name Jeremy Gauna, is a Choctaw Native American and Mexican actor from Texas. Now based in Dallas, he holds 14 credits across television and film, including roles in 1883, 1923, American Primeval, and Blue Ridge: The Series. He began acting after a chance encounter with a film crew in Dallas and trained at R.E.A.C.T. Studio before signing with an agent following a speaking role on Queen of the South.

Q: Who replaced Cole Brings Plenty in 1923 Season 2? A: JP Gauna replaced the late Cole Brings Plenty in the role of Pete Plenty Clouds in 1923 Season 2 on Paramount+. The two men had known each other personally. Gauna received approval from Brings Plenty's family before accepting the role and appeared in six episodes of the season. Co-star Aminah Nieves said of the casting: it could not have been anyone else.

Q: What is JP Gauna in on Netflix? A: JP Gauna plays the character Tall Shadow in American Primeval, a six-episode Netflix limited series that premiered January 9, 2025. The series is set during the Utah War of 1857 and received critical praise for its unflinching portrayal of the American frontier. Gauna appeared across five of the six episodes.

Q: Is JP Gauna actually Native American? A: Yes. JP Gauna is a member of the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma and is also of Mexican heritage. His Indigenous identity is central to the roles he pursues and the mission behind his work. He has spoken publicly about the responsibility of portraying Native stories authentically and the importance of telling uncomfortable histories so they are not repeated.

Q: What did JP Gauna do before acting? A: Before his acting career, JP Gauna spent seven years working in marketing and advertising at The Dallas Morning News in Dallas, Texas. He was also a high school all-state athlete and dual-sport college athlete who played semi-pro basketball in Oklahoma City. He began acting training after a chance encounter with a television film crew and used paid time off from the newspaper to attend classes at R.E.A.C.T. Studio.
